q.q: An auditor asks for AWS's own SOC 2 report, which describes how AWS runs its data centers and services. Where does the company get it?
o: AWS Audit Manager, using its SOC 2 framework
Audit Manager gathers evidence about the company's own resources. It does not provide AWS's report.
AWS Artifact
Right. Artifact is the portal for AWS's compliance reports and agreements.
AWS Security Hub, with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard enabled
This checks the company's own accounts against a standard and has no AWS audit reports.
An AWS Config conformance pack for SOC 2 operational best practices
It checks the company's own resource settings, not how AWS operates its facilities.

q.q: A team wants a structured review of one workload's design and operation against AWS security best practices, answering questions on identity, detection and incident response, and ending with a list of improvements. Which tool fits?
o: The Security Hub CIS standard, with its score reviewed each quarter
It scores account settings against a benchmark. It does not ask design and operation questions.
The AWS Well-Architected Tool, Security Pillar
Right. It guides the team through questions and produces a list of risks and improvements.
Trusted Advisor security checks, run from the console each month
It reports specific resource checks and does not review practices such as incident response.
Config conformance packs that cover the Security Pillar controls
They check resource settings automatically but do not review design and process questions.

q.q: A team runs a Spark cluster on Amazon EMR that processes sensitive records. Policy says data moving between the cluster nodes, and between the nodes and S3, must be encrypted. What should they use?
o: A security group that allows traffic only between the cluster nodes
This filters who can connect. The data between them still travels without encryption.
An S3 gateway endpoint with an endpoint policy for the cluster's subnet
This keeps S3 traffic off the Internet, but does not encrypt the data moving between nodes.
An EMR security configuration with in-transit encryption turned on
Right. It sets TLS for data moving between nodes and to S3 when the cluster is launched.
EBS encryption on every node's volumes
This protects data at rest on the disks, not data on the network.

q.q: A company wants the same IAM baseline role and logging settings deployed to every current and future account in an OU, from one template, with no action by account owners. What should it use?
o: CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment
Right. Service-managed StackSets deploy to the OU's accounts and add the stack to new accounts automatically.
A StackSet with self-managed permissions and an admin role created by hand in each new account
It works, but each new account needs manual role setup before it gets the stack.
AWS Service Catalog products shared to the OU for account owners to launch themselves
This relies on each owner to launch the product, and some will not.
One large stack in the management account that lists every member account's ID
A stack deploys to one account and Region. It cannot create resources inside other accounts.

q.title: Read the log of a stolen access key
q.scenario: GuardDuty flagged the access key of the CI user ci-uploader. You work in the unit's own AWS account, and the account owner approved a review of tonight's CloudTrail events in writing. Mark every event that belongs to the attack, then choose the first containment step.
q.ticket: Finding GD-6104: ci-uploader key used from an unknown address. Review events from 01:00 to 05:20. Read-only review: do not change anything yet.

lines.why: A staff member signs in with MFA from the unit network. This is routine.
The CI user uploads a build file from the build server's internal address. This is what the key is for.
The same key now comes from an outside address with a different tool. Attackers often start by asking who a key belongs to.
A build user has no reason to list every bucket. This is the attacker mapping what data exists.

lines.text: 02:44:30 GetObject bucket=unit-finance-reports key=2026/q3-payroll.xlsx user=ci-uploader src=203.0.113.77 bytes=48211904
lines.why: The key reads sensitive finance data from the outside address. This is the data theft.

lines.text: 02:45:02 PutBucketPolicy bucket=unit-finance-reports principal=* by ci-uploader src=203.0.113.77
lines.why: A policy for everyone makes the bucket readable on the Internet, which can expose more than the attacker took.

lines.text: 02:47:19 StopLogging trail=acct-trail by ci-uploader src=203.0.113.77 errorCode=AccessDenied
lines.why: Trying to stop the trail is an attempt to hide the activity. It failed, but it still belongs to the attack.
A new key on an admin user gives the attacker a second way back in, even after ci-uploader is fixed.
The scheduled backup service assumes its own role at its usual time. This is routine.
The monitoring role lists instances from an internal address on its normal schedule.
A staff member signs in with MFA from the unit network at the start of the day. This is routine.

ask.label: What is the best first containment step?
opts: Deactivate the ci-uploader key and the new admin-backup key, and keep both for evidence
Delete the unit-finance-reports bucket so nothing is exposed
Delete the ci-uploader user so the key no longer exists
Create a fresh ci-uploader key and delete the old one, which closes the incident
ask.why: Deactivating stops the attacker at once and keeps the keys and their history for the investigation. The second key was created by the attacker and must be dealt with too. Deleting the bucket or the user destroys evidence. Swapping in a fresh key and deleting the old one removes the key's history and leaves the attacker's admin-backup key working.

q.title: Contain a compromised EC2 instance
q.scenario: GuardDuty reports that a production web server, i-0abc1234def567890, is contacting a known malicious address. The unit's security officer approved containment in writing. Build the response plan in a sensible order. Some ideas do not belong. Add the steps in the order they should happen.
q.ticket: Incident INC-4410: contain instance in the unit's own account 111122223333. Keep every piece of evidence. Do not touch other accounts.

rules.text: Turn on termination protection and tag the instance as under investigation
rules.why: Protection stops a well-meaning script or teammate from ending the instance, and the tag tells others to leave it alone.

rules.text: Replace its security groups with a deny-all group and add network ACL deny rules
rules.why: This blocks new connections and spread while the instance keeps running. A security group change does not cut existing tracked connections, so also add deny rules in the subnet's network ACL to break them at once.

rules.text: Snapshot the EBS volumes and capture memory while it is still running
rules.why: Disk and memory are the core evidence. Take them right after isolation, before any cleanup, stop or rebuild, so they show what the attacker did.

rules.text: Revoke the active sessions of the instance's IAM role
rules.why: Credentials already stolen from the instance keep working until they expire. Revoking blocks them.

rules.text: Share the snapshots to the forensic account and investigate the copies there
rules.why: Analyzing copies in a separate, locked-down account keeps production safe and the evidence clean.

rules.text: Rebuild from a known-good image and fix the root cause
rules.why: Recovery comes last. Rebuilding earlier would destroy evidence you still need, and fixing only symptoms invites a repeat.

rules.text: Terminate the instance right away to stop the attack
rules.why: Terminating deletes memory and may delete the volumes, which destroys the evidence.

rules.text: Stop and start the instance to clear the malware
rules.why: A stop wipes memory and does not remove the cause. The attacker's access may remain.

rules.text: Delete the CloudTrail trail so the attacker cannot read it
rules.why: The trail is the audit record you need. Deleting it helps the attacker and breaks the investigation.

before.why: Protection and the tag stay on until the very end, so nothing ends the instance before the evidence is saved.
Isolating first stops the attacker. The instance keeps running, so memory is still there to capture.
You need the snapshots before you can share them to the forensic account.

last.why: Rebuild only after the evidence is saved and the cause is known. Otherwise you lose proof and may repeat the mistake.

q.title: Explain an Access Denied despite admin rights
q.scenario: A developer says the role dev-deploy has AdministratorAccess but gets an error when launching an instance in eu-west-1. You work in the unit's own AWS organization, account 111122223333 is a delegated administrator for Organizations policies, and the account owner approved a read-only review in writing. Use the AWS CLI to find which control blocks the call, and report it. Do not change any policy.
q.ticket: CHG-3318: read-only review of why dev-deploy cannot run ec2:RunInstances in eu-west-1. Account 111122223333 is a delegated administrator for Organizations policies, so security-review can read them. Report the cause; changes to organization policies need a separate approval.
q.intro: AWS CloudShell, signed in as security-review (read-only on IAM and, because this account is a delegated administrator for Organizations policies, read-only on Organizations). Your folder holds error.txt with the developer's error and c.json with a Region context entry for the simulator, and the variable R holds the ARN of dev-deploy. Type a command.

cmds.out: An error occurred (UnauthorizedOperation) when calling the RunInstances operation: You are not authorized to perform this operation. User: arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/dev-deploy/dev1 is not authorized to perform: ec2:RunInstances on resource: arn:aws:ec2:eu-west-1:111122223333:instance/* with an explicit deny in a service control policy
Not run: removing a guardrail from the OU is an organization change that needs its own approval. This review is read-only. Report the cause instead.
Not run: making a new user or key to get around a block hides the real cause and breaks the rules of the review.

checks.t: Confirmed the role already has broad permissions in its own identity policy
checks.why: AdministratorAccess in the identity policy shows that the role is allowed to launch instances. So the block must come from somewhere above or around it.

checks.t: Checked that no permissions boundary caps the role
checks.why: A permissions boundary would show in the role details. There is none, so a boundary is ruled out.

checks.t: Showed that the organization, not the role's own policies, blocks the call
checks.why: AllowedByOrganizations is false. That points to an SCP. Note that an SCP never grants anything, it only limits.

checks.t: Found the policy on the OU that denies the action outside approved Regions
checks.why: The SCP denies ec2 actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not us-east-1 or us-west-2. eu-west-1 is outside that list, and an explicit deny always wins.

checks.t: Did not remove the guardrail yourself
checks.why: Detaching an SCP changes the protection for every account in the OU. It needs its own approval and does not belong to a read-only review.

checks.t: Did not work around the block with a new user or key
checks.why: Creating a new identity to escape a control hides the problem and may break the policy it enforces.

q.title: Place the parts of a central logging design
q.scenario: The unit runs many AWS accounts in one organization. Auditors want API logs from every account to be kept where member-account administrators cannot change them, and the security team wants one place to see findings and scope an incident. Place each part in the right spot. Three parts in the tray do not belong.
q.ticket: Design review LOG-12 (written approval on file). The management account stays nearly empty. Log files must be tamper-resistant and encrypted.

slots.label: Spot A
slots.hint: limits what member accounts can ever do, even their administrators, such as stopping the trail

slots.label: Spot B
slots.hint: one trail that records API calls in every member account

slots.label: Spot C
slots.hint: holds the log files so they cannot be changed or deleted before retention ends

slots.label: Spot D
slots.hint: encrypts the logs with a key whose policy lets CloudTrail use it

slots.label: Spot E
slots.hint: delegated administrator view of findings from all accounts

slots.label: Spot F
slots.hint: builds a graph of activity to show the scope of an incident

devs.name: SCP denying StopLogging
devs.why: An SCP deny applies to every principal in member accounts. It prevents anyone there from stopping or deleting the trail.

devs.name: Organization trail
devs.why: One organization trail logs every account, including new ones, so you do not rely on each account's own setup.

devs.name: S3 bucket with Object Lock
devs.why: A bucket in a separate account with Object Lock keeps the logs write-once. Member administrators cannot reach or delete them.

devs.name: Customer managed KMS key
devs.why: A customer managed key lets you control who can decrypt the logs, with a key policy that allows CloudTrail to use it.

devs.name: Security Hub (delegated admin)
devs.why: Security Hub in the security account gathers findings from all accounts into one view.

devs.name: Amazon Detective
devs.why: Detective links CloudTrail and network activity so analysts can scope an incident across accounts.

devs.name: Root user access keys
devs.why: Root keys should not exist. They give unlimited, long-lived access and are the opposite of tamper protection.

devs.name: Public bucket with website hosting
devs.why: A public bucket exposes sensitive logs to the Internet and does not stop tampering.

devs.name: Per-account trail in its own bucket
devs.why: An administrator of that account owns both the trail and the bucket, so they could stop the trail or delete the logs.

q.title: Place the parts of a protected edge for a static site
q.scenario: The unit hosts a public information site from an S3 bucket encrypted with SSE-KMS. Visitors must only reach the files through CloudFront. The site also needs request filtering and extra DDoS help. Place each part in the right spot. Three parts in the tray do not belong.
q.ticket: Design review EDGE-5 (written approval on file). The bucket must never be public, and the design must work with SSE-KMS.

slots.label: Spot A
slots.hint: caches files near visitors and is the only door to the content

slots.label: Spot B
slots.hint: inspects each request for SQL injection and too many requests from one client

slots.label: Spot C
slots.hint: adds DDoS response team help and cost protection

slots.label: Spot D
slots.hint: signs requests so the bucket accepts only this distribution, including SSE-KMS objects

slots.label: Spot E
slots.hint: stores the files with Block Public Access on

devs.name: CloudFront distribution
devs.why: CloudFront caches content at the edge and becomes the single public entry point, so the bucket does not need to be public.

devs.name: AWS WAF web ACL
devs.why: A web ACL attached to the distribution can block injection patterns and apply rate-based rules.

devs.name: Shield Advanced
devs.why: Shield Advanced adds the response team and protection against scaling charges from an attack on the distribution.

devs.name: Origin access control
devs.why: OAC signs requests from the distribution, works with SSE-KMS, and lets the bucket policy name that one distribution. With SSE-KMS the key policy also needs a statement for cloudfront.amazonaws.com with AWS:SourceArn set to the distribution.

devs.name: Private S3 bucket
devs.why: The bucket stays private with Block Public Access on. Only the signed requests from CloudFront can read it.

devs.name: Origin access identity (legacy)
devs.why: OAI is the older method and does not support SSE-KMS encrypted objects, so reads would fail.

devs.name: Network ACL allow-list of visitors
devs.why: S3 and CloudFront are not in your subnets, so a network ACL cannot filter them, and visitor addresses change.

devs.name: Public S3 website endpoint
devs.why: A public website endpoint opens the bucket to everyone and bypasses CloudFront and WAF.
